questions.question: What condition makes two vectors orthogonal?
If nonzero vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfy $x\cdot y>0$, what kind of angle lies between them?
In $\mathbb{R}^n$, at most how many mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors can you have?
Is the zero vector orthogonal to every vector under the dot-product definition?
options: Only in one-dimensional spaces, where every vector is a multiple of it
Yes, its dot product with every vector is zero.
No, because it has no length.

questions.question: Which linear-algebraic property do two nonzero orthogonal vectors necessarily have?
Are $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ orthogonal?
options: Yes, because their dot product is $0$.
No, because both have two nonzero coordinates.
No, because neither vector has length $1$.
Yes, because their coordinate sums are equal.

questions.question: Which vector is orthogonal to $(2,0)$?
For which value of $t$ are $(1,2)$ and $(t,3)$ orthogonal?
What is $(3,4)\cdot(4,-3)$?
Which pair is orthogonal?
Why does orthogonality depend on the inner product being used?
options: The condition is defined through the inner product.
Different inner products give the space a different dimension.
The inner product decides which vector counts as the zero vector.
The condition is $\|x\|=\|y\|$, and norms come from the inner product.

questions.question: If $y$ is a unit vector, what does $x\cdot y$ measure geometrically?
options: The signed length of the projection of $x$ onto $y$.
The unsigned length of the projection of $x$ onto $y$.
The area of the parallelogram spanned by $x$ and $y$.
The cosine of the angle between $x$ and $y$.

questions.question: Can two nonzero orthogonal vectors be scalar multiples of each other?
options: Yes, if their norms are equal.
Yes, every orthogonal pair is made of scalar multiples.
No, except the zero scalar would make one vector zero.
Only if both are unit vectors.

questions.question: Find a vector orthogonal to $(1,2,3)$.
For which value of $a$ are $(a,1)$ and $(2,4)$ orthogonal?
If $u=(1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})$ and $v=(1/\sqrt{2},-1/\sqrt{2})$, what is $u\cdot v$?
Why is it safer to define orthogonality by $x\cdot y=0$ rather than by drawing a right angle?
options: The dot-product condition works in any dimension
The dot product gives the angle in degrees directly
Right angles can only be defined for vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$
The dot-product condition excludes the zero vector by design

questions.question: What subtlety arises with the zero vector and the phrase “right angle”?
options: The zero vector is orthogonal by dot product but has no direction
The zero vector makes a $90^\circ$ angle with every vector by definition
The zero vector is orthogonal only to itself, not to other vectors
The zero vector is excluded since $\boldsymbol0\cdot y$ is undefined
